integration_questions: With wheel_track at 0.14 m, does the robot still turn sharply enough on the slalom, or does line loss rise at the tightest bends?
Which kp and kd range is stable at this track width, and does the wider track allow higher kp without oscillation on the oval?
Does max_error peak at the same point on the s-bend and slalom as before, and does line loss occur at that point?
Which sensors carry most of the signal, and can the outer sensors (x = +/-0.06 m) be given smaller weights to reduce line loss?
feedback_request.requested_format: Brief notes on each question, plus the single geometry change you would make first if you could change only one thing.

intent: Isolate the wheel-track effect in the opposite direction to iteration 3. Keep the iteration 1 layout (7 sensors, 0.02 m spacing, span +/-0.06 m, 16 mm footprints, y=0.06 m, mass 0.6 kg, radius 0.03 m, body 0.16 x 0.12 m) and change only wheel_track from 0.12 to 0.14 m. Expect a lower yaw gain per PWM unit, less overshoot on bends, fewer off-track ends on the s-bend and slalom, and a score at or above 482.7. If the score falls, the track is at its optimum near 0.12 m and the next lever is sensing.
learning: Iterations 2 and 3 both used a 0.10 m track and both scored below iteration 1, so narrower track is harmful for this controller family. Hypotheses to test: (1) a wider track of 0.14 m reduces bend overshoot and raises s-bend completions; (2) the 0.12 m track is near optimal, and the limit is then sensing; (3) the 0.14 m track may slow the slalom turn enough to raise line loss there. Measurements to request on each development track: completion, progress, completion_time, max_error, rms_error, line_loss_events, steering_oscillation and control_effort.
rationale: Race evidence so far: iteration 1 (7 sensors at 0.02 m spacing spanning +/-0.06 m, 16 mm footprints, y=0.06 m, mass 0.6 kg, wheel_track 0.12 m) scored 482.7, the best so far. Oval finished 20/20. Every bend failure is an off-track end with max_error at or above 0.06 m, while rms_error stays small (0.023 to 0.030 m), so the problem is occasional large excursions on bends, not steady tracking error. Iteration 3 changed only wheel_track to 0.10 m and scored 357.3, a clear drop: s-bend completions fell from 5/20 to 1/20 and oval finishes from 20/20 to 14/20, with max_error reaching the limit on more runs. Iteration 2 also used 0.10 m and scored lower (411.7). So a narrower track, which gives more yaw per PWM unit, makes the robot more aggressive and it overshoots on bends. That points the other way: a wider track should reduce yaw gain per unit of steering command, so bend excursions should be damped. Body width has no effect on the off-track limit (it stays 0.06 m across the allowed range), so drivetrain and sensing remain the only levers. I therefore keep the iteration 1 layout and change one variable: wheel_track from 0.12 to 0.14 m. This is a clean test of the monotonic trend (0.10 hurt, so 0.14 should help if the trend holds). Expected result: fewer off-track ends on the s-bend and slalom, max_error below 0.06 m on more runs, and a score at or above 482.7. Main risk: a wider track adds yaw inertia relative to turn authority, so the robot may be too slow to turn on the sharpest slalom bends and line loss may rise there.
